summary: You solved Two Sum cleanly with the canonical optimal single-pass hash map approach and passed all tests. Your reasoning covered the key pitfalls (no self-use, handling duplicates) and you accurately stated time/space complexity and a solid sorted-array follow-up.

test_results.summary_note: All visible and hidden tests passed; no failures reported.

dimensions.name: Correctness & Completeness
dimensions.label: strong
dimensions.what_went_well: Returned correct indices for all cases; the check-complement-before-insert ordering prevents using the same element twice and correctly handles duplicates like [3,3] with target 6.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Add (or be ready to discuss) an explicit error/exception strategy for cases where the guarantee is removed (e.g., no solution or multiple solutions), even if the current prompt guarantees exactly one.

dimensions.name: Problem-Solving & Thinking
dimensions.label: strong
dimensions.what_went_well: You quickly identified the brute force baseline and then moved to the optimal pattern with a clear invariant: map contains prior elements only, so matches never reuse the current index.
dimensions.what_to_improve: When time allows, articulate the invariant in one crisp sentence up front (e.g., “seen holds indices < i”), which makes correctness proofs even tighter.

dimensions.name: Technical Communication
dimensions.label: strong
dimensions.what_went_well: You communicated tradeoffs (O(n^2) vs O(n)), narrated the key implementation detail (check then insert), and did a quick trace on an example to validate behavior.
dimensions.what_to_improve: In follow-ups, briefly call out any constraints needed for the alternate approach (e.g., two pointers requires sorted input; if not sorted, you’d need to sort and manage original indices).

dimensions.name: Complexity & Optimization
dimensions.label: strong
dimensions.what_went_well: Your complexity claims match the answer key: O(n) time with amortized O(1) hash operations and O(n) space; you also gave the sorted-array two-pointer optimization to O(1) extra space.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Be prepared to mention worst-case hash map behavior (rare in practice, but interviewers sometimes probe) and why it’s acceptable under typical assumptions.

dimensions.name: Code Quality
dimensions.label: strong
dimensions.what_went_well: The implementation is concise, readable, and idiomatic Python; variable names are clear and control flow is straightforward.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Consider returning a tuple instead of a list (or documenting the choice) if a specific output type is required by a platform; also consider omitting the final return [] if the guarantee always holds, or raising an error for clarity.

dimensions.name: Independence
dimensions.label: strong
dimensions.what_went_well: You reached the optimal solution without hints and independently handled common pitfalls (self-pairing and duplicates).
dimensions.what_to_improve: Stretch goal: proactively propose and compare 2–3 solution routes (brute force, hash map, sorting + two pointers with index tracking) and justify why you choose one given constraints.

thinking_and_logic: You followed the expected progression: establish the O(n^2) brute force baseline, then choose the canonical O(n) single-pass hash map approach. The key logic is checking for the complement in previously seen values before inserting the current value, which enforces the “don’t reuse the same element” constraint and correctly supports duplicates.
code_assessment: Your final code matches the answer key’s optimal solution: a single pass storing value→index and returning as soon as a complement is found. Compared with non-optimal alternatives (nested loops or sorting-first approaches that can lose original indices), your solution achieves optimal time (O(n)) while maintaining correct original indices and handling duplicates robustly.

transcript.text: Here's the problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Take your time to read it.
Okay. Quick clarification — is there always exactly one valid answer, and can I use the same element twice?
Exactly one valid answer exists, and you may not use the same element twice.

Got it. The brute force is checking every pair, which is O(n squared). But I can do better with a hash map: as I scan, I store each value with its index, and for each element I check whether target minus the current value is already in the map. That's a single pass, O(n) time, O(n) space. I'll go with that.
Writing it now. I'm checking the complement before inserting the current value so I never match an element with itself. That also handles duplicates like two threes summing to six.
Done. Let me trace it with nums = [2, 7, 11, 15], target 9: i=0 stores 2, i=1 complement is 2 which is in the map, so I return [0, 1]. I'll run the tests.
All visible tests pass. Can you state the complexity of your solution?
Time is O(n) — one pass, each lookup and insert is amortized O(1). Space is O(n) for the map in the worst case.
Follow-up: what would you change if the input array were sorted?
Then I'd use two pointers from both ends and move them inward based on whether the sum is too big or too small. That keeps O(n) time but drops the extra space to O(1).
Great. That wraps up the interview.
